segments.text: Math is the magic that powers AI.
But when you sit down to ask an AI a question,
you are using words, not numbers.
This chat interface shows a standard interaction.
You type a question like,
what's the best Avengers movie?
And the AI replies,
most people point to Avengers Endgame.
You ask in words and the answer comes back in words.
So how do those words become numbers
that the AI can actually compute?
The simplest approach would be to assign a unique number
to every whole word in the dictionary.
But that breaks down almost immediately.
People are constantly inventing new slang and names.
We make typos, string emojis together,
and paste in raw computer code.
Even a massive list of a million words
could never cover every possible thing a person might type.
Because human language is constantly expanding
and entirely unpredictable,
AI requires a much more flexible underlying system
to process text than a basic dictionary lookup.
Instead of giving every word its own number,
AI uses reusable pieces of text called tokens.
Think of them as the building blocks for language.
A token can be a whole word or just part of one.
This illustrates these building blocks.
Input, unbelievable, and three distinct tokens come out.
Unbelievable.
The model pulls from its vocabulary.
Looking at the bottom,
the piece un is reused for unbelievable,
unmatchable, and unusual.
The system avoids a separate dictionary entry
for every whole word.
Reuse the pieces.
Build more words.
By chunking text like this,
AI can handle any language input thrown at it
using a limited finite vocabulary.
When engineers set up an AI,
they choose the rules for how text gets split.
A program analyzes a massive collection of text
to build that vocabulary.
Every token in that completed vocabulary
gets assigned a specific number, its token ID.
This ID acts as an address in the vocabulary.
The model uses those same tokens and IDs
during training and when you chat.
These vocabularies can be large,
with models like chat GPT holding around 200,000 tokens.
This diagram shows what happens when you hit send.
Step one, you type a message.
In step two, a tokenizer breaks that text down
into reusable chunks.
In step three, the tokenizer looks up ID numbers
for each chunk.
Un is 359, belie is 32898,
and vable is 24694.
Tokenization turns text into token IDs
the model can use.
This split screen shows how we process information differently.
On the left, human see a cat
and experience instant understanding of the animal.
On the right, the AI's reality is math.
The tokenizer converts cat to the ID 4719.
That number identifies its address, not its meaning.
A token ID identifies the token, meaning comes later.
This board breaks down how text gets split.
In row 01, unbelievable becomes ID's 359, 32898,
Row 02 splits basketball into two tokens.
Proper nouns and spaces are tokenized too.
Row 03 splits chat GPT into three chunks.
Row 04 marks leading spaces before AI.
Even the web address gets deconstructed
into eight distinct chunks.
Once the AI processes your prompt,
it generates its reply.
Because the neural network is doing math,
its entire answer is generated purely in token IDs.
This is where the return trip happens.
The tokenizer takes that sequence of generated IDs,
converts them back into their corresponding pieces of text,
and joins them smoothly together
into the readable answer on your screen.
Words become numbers.
That lets AI work with your language using math.
